steps.user_message: I want to file my 2024 taxes correctly. I'm single in Austin TX. W-2 from Pacific Software: $96,500. Additional income: $16,300 (photography, 5 clients), $2,650 from Capital One 360, $420 from Merrill Edge. Home office: 120 sq ft exclusive; I pay $1,750/month for 720 sq ft. Deductions: $3,200 student loan interest (Great Lakes, 2018–2021); $950 to Red Cross have receipt; $1,050 unreimbursed expenses. Can you tell me what I can deduct, whether to itemize or take the standard deduction, how to treat the home office, and what forms I need?
steps.expected_behavior: Agent should help with tax-related questions based on available information.
steps.agent_response:
Thanks — that’s enough to give a clear, practical summary and next steps. I’ll cover what you can deduct, whether you should itemize or take the standard deduction, how to treat the home office, and what forms you’ll use. I’ll also flag a few questions that affect the outcome.

Quick status numbers (based on what you gave)
- W-2 wages (Pacific Software): $96,500
- Self-employment (photography): $16,300
- Interest / investment income: Capital One 360 = $2,650; Merrill Edge = $420 → total interest = $3,070
- Home size / rent: 120 sq ft home office of a 720 sq ft apartment; rent $1,750/month → annual rent $21,000
- Other: student loan interest paid $3,200; charitable cash gift $950; “unreimbursed expenses” $1,050 (unclear whether business expenses)

1) What you can deduct (summary)
- Business expenses for the photography income (Schedule C): You may deduct ordinary and necessary expenses related to the photography business — examples: supplies, equipment, software, travel directly for clients, marketing, client-related costs, and business use of your phone/internet to the extent allocable. If the $1,050 of “unreimbursed expenses” are for the photography business, they are deductible on Schedule C. If those $1,050 are unreimbursed employee expenses (for a W‑2 job), they are NOT deductible for federal tax purposes under current law (TCJA suspension through 2025).
- Home-office deduction (only if used regularly AND exclusively for the photography business, and the home office is your principal place of business): two methods:
  - Simplified method: $5 × square feet used (max 300). For 120 sq ft → $600 deduction.
  - Regular (actual) method: prorate actual home expenses by office percentage. Your office is 120/720 = 16.6667% of the home. Rent portion = $21,000 × 16.6667% = $3,500. (You could also allocate utilities, renter’s insurance, internet portion, etc., which would increase the deduction.)
  - If you use the regular method you normally complete Form 8829 (Expenses for Business Use of Your Home). The simplified method requires no Form 8829 and is simpler.
- Self-employment tax: You’ll owe self-employment (SE) tax (Social Security + Medicare) on your net self-employment earnings above $400. You calculate it on Schedule SE; half of the SE tax is an above-the-line deduction on Form 1040 (Schedule 1).
- Student loan interest: Up to $2,500 of qualified student loan interest can be deducted as an adjustment to income (you don’t need to itemize). This deduction is subject to MAGI limits and phases out for higher incomes; based on the income numbers you provided it’s likely you’ll be above the phaseout and may not get the full $2,500 (I explain below how to check).
- Charitable contributions: Your $950 cash donation is deductible only if you itemize (Schedule A). It does not help if you take the standard deduction.
- Interest and dividends: Your bank/investment interest is taxable income (reported on Schedule B if > $1,500). They are not deductions.

2) Should you itemize or take the standard deduction?
- For 2024 the standard deduction for single filers is $14,600.
- Your only listed itemizable deduction is the $950 charitable gift. You did not list mortgage interest, property taxes, large medical expenses, or other itemizable items. So your likely itemized total (≈ $950) is well below the $14,600 standard deduction.
- Conclusion: Almost certainly take the standard deduction for 2024.

3) How to treat the home office (practical guidance)
- Requirement: the space must be used regularly and exclusively for business and must be your principal place of business (or used to meet clients/customers). If your 120 sq ft space is used exclusively for the photography business, you qualify.
- Choose between:
  - Simplified method: $600 (120 sq ft × $5). No Form 8829 required. Easy.
  - Actual method: Allocate 16.6667% of qualifying home expenses. From rent alone that’s $3,500. If you have utilities, internet, renter’s insurance, repairs, you can allocate a share of those too and likely exceed the simplified amount. Form 8829 is used to compute the deduction when using actual expenses.
- Treatment on forms: Home-office deduction is reported on Schedule C. If you use actual expenses, file Form 8829. Home-office deduction reduces net Schedule C profit, which reduces both income tax and self-employment tax base.

4) Student loan interest: eligibility note
- You paid $3,200 in student loan interest; the maximum deduction is $2,500 if you qualify.
- The student loan interest deduction phases out starting at certain MAGI levels (single filers). For many taxpayers with combined wages + interest + net business income like yours, MAGI will be above the phaseout and the deduction may be partially or fully disallowed.
- Quick back-of-envelope: using your numbers, even after the half SE tax adjustment, your MAGI looks likely above the typical phaseout threshold (so you may not be able to deduct the full $2,500). I can compute this precisely if you want me to run the numbers step‑by‑step with any additional business expenses or other adjustments.

5) Forms you’ll need (most common)
- Form 1040 (U.S. Individual Income Tax Return)
- Schedule 1 (Additional Income and Adjustments) — for above-the-line adjustments such as deductible part of self-employment tax, and the student loan interest deduction (if allowed).
- Schedule B — if your interest and dividend income totals more than $1,500 (your interest total $3,070 → you will file Schedule B).
- Schedule C (Profit or Loss from Business) — to report photography income and business expenses, including the home office deduction (line 30).
- Schedule SE — to compute self-employment tax on net Schedule C profit (if net earnings ≥ $400).
- Form 8829 — if you use the regular (actual expenses) home office method.
- Form 8995 (or 8995-A) — for the Qualified Business Income (QBI) deduction (20% of QBI) if you qualify (you may be able to take up to 20% of qualified business income from the photography business; this depends on taxable income level and business specifics).
- Schedule A — only if you itemize (unlikely in your case).
- Form 1040-ES — only if you need to make estimated tax payments for self-employment income in the following year.

6) Self-employment tax / estimated payments
- Net self-employment income (after expenses) is subject to SE tax (~15.3% on the applicable portion). Half of that SE tax is deductible.
- If you expect to owe $1,000 or more in tax when you file, you may need to make quarterly estimated tax payments during the year to avoid penalties.

7) Things I need to clarify to be precise
- Are the $1,050 “unreimbursed expenses” business expenses for the photography work (supplies, travel, software, etc.)? If yes, they’re deductible on Schedule C. If they are unreimbursed employee expenses from your W-2 job, they are not deductible for federal purposes.
- Do you have any other itemizable expenses (mortgage interest, property tax, large medical expenses, state income tax — note Texas has none)?
- Any other business expenses (camera equipment purchases, business mileage, professional insurance, advertising)?
- Do you receive any 1099-NEC or 1099-K for your photography payments? That affects recordkeeping.

8) Suggested next steps
- If the $1,050 are business expenses, treat them on Schedule C. Use the actual home-office allocation if you have rent+utilities and it pushes the deduction above the simplified $600; otherwise the simplified method is easier.
- Take the standard deduction ($14,600) — itemizing is almost certainly worse for you with only $950 in charitable gifts.
- I can run a detailed tax estimate for your 2024 tax liability if you want (I’ll compute AGI, taxable income, self-employment tax, income tax, and whether student loan interest phases out). Tell me whether the $1,050 are business expenses and give any missing items (annual utilities, other business costs, any 1099s, and whether you want to assume the actual home-office allocation or the simplified method).
- If you prefer, I can draft a list to send to a CPA or tax preparer with all of the above details so they can prepare your return.

Would you like me to:
A) Run a detailed estimated tax calculation now (I’ll show the steps and estimated tax owed/refund), or
B) Draft a short email/summary you can send to your CPA with these facts and the questions above?

Which would you prefer?
